I thought this puzzle really shined with some of its short misdirections—well-funded group, stock exchange, theater directors—these are some of the clues that make my day even more than the long ones.

My favorite part of this puzzle is the catchy longs – A BET IS A BET, DOGGONE IT, NO ONE CARES, DO ME A SOLID, HANG ON A SEC, BE RIGHT BACK.

There is NO END to the number of long answers that can go into the grid, and Aidan has a great eye, IMO, for finding longs that are fun and relatable, that elevate the solving experience.  The ones I just mentioned are not only catchy, but fresh – all of these have appeared in the Times puzzle twice before or less.

I also liked the fauna vibe in the box, with MOOS, CAT LADY, DOGGONE IT, ARK, and IBIS.  That last one goes well with CANES, as the ibis is the University of Miami’s mascot.  

For me, Aidan, this had a lovely combination of splat-fills and stop-and-thinks, and got me in a great mood.  Thank you for all you put into this!

Just learned today that Mann's works are all now in the public domain and that there is at least one new translation  available as part of the Oxford World’s Classics series.

Meanwhile, I leave with a thought that the Waterfall scene echoes the Wolf's Lair scene in the opera Der Freischütz where the protagonist makes a deal with the devil that lets him win the contest and also eliminates his rival.

@Al  in Pittsburgh
Hi, Al, long time no see. What are you reading these days?

If you happen to catch the game on Saturday, and the camera happens to catch in the crowd a politely cheering but ultimately stoic man laying a calming hand on a wildly emoting woman who’s already yelled herself hoarse with more invectives hurled in the 1st quarter at BYU, the refs, and possibly Fate than normally come out of her mouth in a year—uh, yes, you’ll see how good my husband looks in red. 

I had to look up what happens in Der Freischütz. It is the same theme of the good or the intellectual or both being foiled by the irrational, isn’t it? Be it the force of a waterfall or someone like Peeperkorn or Samiel. It was Mann’s view of what happens when man meets Nature—Death in Venice, too, is a primer in it—shared by most of the Romantics, and, not the least thanks to Mann, by me as well. As for magic, the supernatural (I just watched the Wolf’s Lair scene; it’s magnificent), aren’t these just words we humans have coined to explain Nature away?

The Magic Mountain stays with you, doesn’t it?

Thanks for the heads up on the translations of Mann and his work entering the public domain. It’s always nice when instant literary gratification is available online. 

I’m currently in thrall to and devouring V.S. Naipaul, but I took a break when my library hold on Bulgakov’s The Master and Margarita came in. If you haven’t read either gentleman, hie thee to the nearest library app, I say.

I didn't want to lose the German vibe so I'm rereading my copy of Walter Kaufman's bilingual edition of Faust. (Slow going.  I keep foolishly trying and stumbling with the German text.)  His Introduction has a lot to say about Goethe which is applicable to Mann.  "The more incommensurable and incomprehensible for the understanding a poetic creation may be, the better" is a direct quote from Goethe. 

I think that Mann wanted to be seen as a 20th Century Goethe for the German people.

He was talented enough.

Bilingual editions are so tempting sometimes but bears to get through unless you’re really fluent.

For a slightly lighter German-speaking writer, have you considered Stefan Zweig? He’s Austrian so he gets a pass into the club, but supernatural battles needn’t be fought.

I get it where you're coming from! But even puzzlemakers who use construction software still have to flex their creative muscles and bring personality to their puzzles. To address some of your very good questions:

- Using someone else's grid design (or tweaking it slightly) is an accepted practice, as the same grid skeleton can produce many different puzzles. Still, the practice has its limits: the editors probably aren't going to be excited about a grid design if they've seen it hundreds of times already. 

- All constructors start with an off-the-shelf wordlist; they then add fun words and colorful phrases they encounter to their lists, looking for unique entries to make their puzzles fresh. As Aidan mentioned, his scored wordlist is curated too: He's deciding which words he personally wants in a puzzle, which brings his unique sensibilities to it. 

- Fill generation is a super useful feature for constructors — but it still requires human curation. The software doesn't know about Naticks, or too many proper nouns, or fun connections that make for an enjoyable solve: BE RIGHT BACK standing next to HANG ON A SEC, for instance. 

- Finally, don't forget about the clues! Construction software does not write the clues for you, so cluewriting is another way for constructors to get creative and showcase their personal voice. 

Hope this helps!

Sean was on my wavelength but just to hopefully quell some concern, the constructor note might have undersold my involvement in the final product! The word scoring has taken dozens or hundreds of hours and I haven’t used any algorithms to do it, it’s just me looking through entries and using human judgment. I also always defer to human judgment for the short entries when there are enough possibilities to consider (maybe on the order of tens) that a mere mortal like me can process them all. I believe in this specific grid I eventually placed BEST COAST because it was especially fun and seemed to fill well, and then Ingrid’s main job was to give me the resulting list of possible entries in each long slot which could fit as a result. I picked the combination that seemed best from there (which used some heuristics besides simply word score, like the ability to give the same clues to two pairs of consecutive entries) and finishing up the short fill from there wasn’t too bad. 

Ultimately I like to think of my setup as reducing the search space of good grids so that my human judgment can find something neat more easily. If I didn’t use computer assistance in this way, I think it would be much more challenging to be satisfied with every long entry. But others might reasonably argue that the result feels less personal - so there certainly isn’t a right way to go about any of this. In fact, many NYT themelesses are probably made with less computer assistance than this one.

Cheers!
